title: grep
description: GNU grep — print lines that match a pattern. The classic POSIX/GNU command-line tool for searching plain-text data sets for lines matching a regular expression, ships by default on virtually every Linux and Unix-like system.

Getting Started.Getting Started:
`grep` is part of GNU coreutils-adjacent tooling and ships preinstalled on
almost every Linux distribution and macOS (as an older BSD variant unless you
install GNU grep separately). There is nothing to configure — it's a single
binary that reads from files or standard input.

The current stable release of GNU grep is **3.12**. Releases are
infrequent and mostly consist of bug fixes and portability work rather than
new features — the core flag surface documented here has been stable for a
very long time, so this guide applies to any recent 3.x release.

## Check what you have

```bash
grep --version
```

On Arch Linux, GNU grep is part of the base system and is installed by
default via the `glibc`/`grep` package:

```bash
sudo pacman -S grep
```

On macOS, the preinstalled `grep` is BSD grep. To get GNU grep's extra
features (like `-P` for Perl regex or `--include`), install it via Homebrew:

```bash
brew install grep
```

This installs it as `ggrep` to avoid clobbering the system binary.

## Your first search

```bash
grep "error" server.log
```

This prints every line in `server.log` containing the literal text `error`.

## Basic syntax

```bash
grep [OPTIONS] PATTERN [FILE...]
```

- `PATTERN` is a regular expression (basic regex by default).
- `FILE...` is zero or more files. If omitted, `grep` reads from stdin.
- If multiple files are given, matching lines are prefixed with the
  filename automatically.

```bash
cat access.log | grep "404"
grep "TODO" src/*.dart
```

See [Core Concepts](/grep/core-concepts/) for how matching, regex flavors,
and exit codes work together.
Getting Started.Core Concepts:
## Exit status

`grep`'s exit code is meaningful and commonly used in scripts:

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | At least one line matched. |
| `1` | No lines matched. |
| `2` | An error occurred (bad option, unreadable file). |

```bash
if grep -q "ERROR" app.log; then
  echo "Errors found"
fi
```

`-q` (quiet) suppresses output entirely and is the idiomatic way to use
`grep` purely for its exit status.

## Regex flavors

`grep` supports three regex dialects, selected by flag:

| Flag | Dialect | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *(default)* | Basic Regular Expressions (BRE) | `\(`, `\)`, `\{`, `\}` needed for grouping/braces. |
| `-E` / `--extended-regexp` | Extended Regular Expressions (ERE) | `(`, `)`, `{`, `}`, `+`, `?`, `\|` work unescaped. Same as `egrep`. |
| `-P` / `--perl-regexp` | Perl-Compatible Regular Expressions (PCRE) | Lookahead/lookbehind, `\d`, `\w`, non-greedy `*?`. GNU grep only, needs libpcre. |
| `-F` / `--fixed-strings` | No regex at all | Pattern(s) are literal strings. Same as `fgrep`. Fastest option for literal searches. |

```bash
# BRE: parentheses must be escaped to group
grep '\(foo\|bar\)' file.txt

# ERE: same thing, cleaner syntax
grep -E '(foo|bar)' file.txt

# PCRE: lookahead
grep -P '(?<=user=)\w+' access.log

# Fixed string: no regex interpretation at all
grep -F 'a.b[c]' file.txt
```

## How matching works

By default `grep` operates line by line: a line either matches the pattern
somewhere within it, or it doesn't. There's no concept of matching across
line boundaries unless you use `-z`/`--null-data` (treat input as
NUL-separated "lines," useful for filenames from `find -print0`) or
`-P` with `(?s)` for a Perl multi-line trick.

Anchors `^` and `$` refer to the start/end of each line, not the whole
input.

## Case sensitivity and word boundaries

```bash
grep -i "warning" log.txt        # case-insensitive
grep -w "cat" file.txt           # whole word only (not "category")
grep -x "done" file.txt          # entire line must match exactly
```

See [Pattern Matching & Regex](/grep/pattern-matching-regex/) for the full
regex syntax reference and [Common Options](/grep/common-options/) for the
rest of the flag surface.

Guides.Pattern Matching & Regex:
This page is a syntax reference for the regex features `grep` understands
in each mode. See [Core Concepts](/grep/core-concepts/) for when to use
which mode.

## BRE / ERE metacharacters

| Meaning | BRE | ERE |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Any character | `.` | `.` |
| Zero or more | `*` | `*` |
| One or more | `\+` (GNU ext.) | `+` |
| Zero or one | `\?` (GNU ext.) | `?` |
| Grouping | `\( \)` | `( )` |
| Alternation | `\\|` | `\|` |
| Bounded repeat | `\{m,n\}` | `{m,n}` |
| Start of line | `^` | `^` |
| End of line | `$` | `$` |
| Character class | `[abc]`, `[^abc]`, `[a-z]` | same |

## Common character classes (POSIX)

```
[[:alpha:]]   letters
[[:digit:]]   digits
[[:alnum:]]   letters and digits
[[:space:]]   whitespace
[[:upper:]]   uppercase letters
[[:lower:]]   lowercase letters
[[:punct:]]   punctuation
```

These are locale-aware, unlike `\w`/`\d`, and work in BRE/ERE without `-P`:

```bash
grep -E '^[[:digit:]]+$' numbers.txt
```

## PCRE-only features (`-P`)

```bash
\d  \D   digit / non-digit
\w  \W   word char / non-word char
\s  \S   whitespace / non-whitespace
(?=...)    lookahead
(?!...)    negative lookahead
(?<=...)   lookbehind
(?<!...)   negative lookbehind
*?  +?     non-greedy quantifiers
```

```bash
# Match "foo" only when followed by "bar", without including "bar" in the match
grep -P 'foo(?=bar)' file.txt

# Extract IPv4-looking tokens
grep -oP '\d{1,3}(\.\d{1,3}){3}' access.log
```

`-o`/`--only-matching` prints just the matched portion of the line rather
than the whole line — extremely useful combined with `-P` for extraction
one-liners.

## Multiple patterns

```bash
grep -e "foo" -e "bar" file.txt      # match foo OR bar
grep -f patterns.txt file.txt        # patterns.txt: one pattern per line
```
Guides.Common Options:
A practical reference of the options used day to day. Run `man grep` or
`grep --help` for the exhaustive list — GNU grep has well over 40 flags.

## Matching behavior

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `-i` | Case-insensitive match. |
| `-v` | Invert match — print non-matching lines. |
| `-w` | Match whole words only. |
| `-x` | Match whole lines only. |
| `-E` | Extended regex. |
| `-F` | Fixed strings (no regex). |
| `-P` | Perl-compatible regex. |
| `-e PATTERN` | Specify pattern explicitly (allows multiple `-e`). |
| `-f FILE` | Read patterns from a file, one per line. |

## Output control

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `-n` | Show line numbers. |
| `-c` | Print only a count of matching lines per file. |
| `-l` | Print only filenames that contain a match. |
| `-L` | Print only filenames that do *not* contain a match. |
| `-o` | Print only the matched text, not the whole line. |
| `-q` | Suppress output; use only the exit status. |
| `-H` | Always print filename, even for a single file. |
| `-h` | Never print filename. |
| `--color=auto` | Highlight matches (often aliased on by default). |

## Context lines

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `-A NUM` | Print NUM lines *after* each match. |
| `-B NUM` | Print NUM lines *before* each match. |
| `-C NUM` | Print NUM lines of context on both sides. |

```bash
grep -C 3 "panic" kernel.log
```

## Recursive & file selection

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `-r` | Recurse into directories. |
| `-R` | Recurse, following symlinks too. |
| `--include=GLOB` | Only search files matching GLOB. |
| `--exclude=GLOB` | Skip files matching GLOB. |
| `--exclude-dir=GLOB` | Skip directories matching GLOB. |
| `-I` | Ignore binary files (same as `--binary-files=without-match`). |

```bash
grep -r --include="*.dart" "TODO" lib/
grep -r --exclude-dir=.git "FIXME" .
```

Note: plain `grep -r` does **not** respect `.gitignore`. For that behavior,
most people reach for `ripgrep` instead — see the companion ripgrep docs.

## Combining flags

Short flags combine naturally:

```bash
grep -rniw "todo" src/
```

is `--recursive --line-number --ignore-case --word-regexp`.

See [Recipes](/grep/recipes/) for these assembled into real workflows.
Guides.Recipes:
Task-oriented one-liners. See [Common Options](/grep/common-options/) for
what each flag does individually.

## Find TODOs across a codebase

```bash
grep -rn --include="*.dart" "TODO\|FIXME" lib/ test/
```

## Case-insensitive search excluding version control

```bash
grep -rin --exclude-dir={.git,.dart_tool,build} "connection refused" .
```

## Count occurrences per file

```bash
grep -rc "import 'package:" lib/ | grep -v ':0'
```

The trailing `grep -v ':0'` drops files with zero matches, since `-c`
always prints a line per file even when the count is zero.

## List files that contain (or don't contain) a pattern

```bash
grep -rl "class .* extends StatelessWidget" lib/    # files that DO
grep -rL "// Copyright" lib/                          # files that DON'T
```

## Use grep as a boolean check in a script

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
if grep -q "^DART_SDK=" .env; then
  echo "DART_SDK already configured"
else
  echo "DART_SDK=\$(which dart)" >> .env
fi
```

## Search compressed logs without decompressing first

```bash
zgrep "OutOfMemoryError" /var/log/app/*.log.gz
```

`zgrep`, `zegrep`, `zfgrep` are thin wrappers that decompress on the fly.

## Extract structured data with -o and -P

```bash
# Pull every email-looking string out of a file
grep -oP '[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.-]+' contacts.txt

# Pull version numbers like "1.2.3" out of a changelog
grep -oE '[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+' CHANGELOG.md
```

## Pipe chains

```bash
ps aux | grep -i dart | grep -v grep
journalctl -u myservice --since today | grep -i error
```

The `grep -v grep` trick filters out the `grep` process itself from
`ps aux` output — a very old but still common idiom.

## Diff-friendly context search

```bash
grep -n -B2 -A5 "throw Exception" lib/**/*.dart
```

Project.FAQ:
### `grep`, `egrep`, `fgrep` — what's the difference?

They're the same binary. `egrep` is equivalent to `grep -E`, and `fgrep` is
equivalent to `grep -F`. Both are considered legacy/deprecated spellings by
GNU grep in favor of the explicit flags, though they still work on most
systems.

### Why doesn't `+`, `?`, or `|` work in my pattern?

You're using Basic Regular Expressions (the default mode), where those are
literal characters. Either escape them (`\+`, `\?`, `\|`) or switch to
`-E` for Extended Regular Expressions where they're metacharacters
natively. See [Pattern Matching & Regex](/grep/pattern-matching-regex/).

### How do I search for a literal `.` or other special character?

Escape it with a backslash (`\.`) in regex mode, or use `-F` to disable
regex interpretation entirely for the whole pattern.

### Does `grep -r` respect `.gitignore`?

No. GNU grep's recursive mode walks the filesystem as-is; it has no concept
of `.gitignore`. If you want gitignore-aware recursive search, use
`git grep` (inside a repo) or `ripgrep`.

### How do I make grep faster on huge files?

- Use `-F` if you don't need regex — literal-string matching is
  substantially faster.
- Avoid `-P` (PCRE) for very large inputs where possible; it's more
  powerful but slower than BRE/ERE for simple patterns.
- `LC_ALL=C grep ...` can meaningfully speed up ASCII-only searches by
  avoiding locale-aware collation.

### Can grep search binary files?

By default `grep` detects binary files and reports only whether they
match (`Binary file X matches`), rather than printing lines. Force
text-mode scanning with `-a`/`--text`, or skip binaries entirely with
`-I`.

### Where's the changelog / how do I report a bug?

GNU grep is maintained as part of the GNU project. See
[GNU grep on savannah.gnu.org](https://savannah.gnu.org/projects/grep/)
and the [GNU grep manual](https://www.gnu.org/software/grep/manual/grep.html).
